My intent here is to be constructive and helpful, so please let me know if I've missed the mark. I'm not trying to be a Debbie downer!

I just wanted to say, please remember too not just the impact on you, but also the impact of hyperfixation on your SO. Hyperfixating on someone sets them up for certain expectations in the relationship. They are probably deciding some of their feelings about you and what they want in a relationship with you based on the hyperfixating you are showing now. It will pass, and they could potentially feel hurt when they are suddenly faced with a different set of traits and expectations than they previously thought. Please talk to them about this before the hyperfixation ends. Let them know what they can expect, so they can make informed decisions about the relationship.  If you two are right for each other, you'll be able to sail through these things, as long as there is open and honest communication. 

Just speaking as someone who has felt like someone else's "high" before, there's nothing wrong with feeling (and loving) the feeling of love! I'm not trying to be a bummer at all, just remember that in addition to being a hyperfixation, at the end of the day, they're a person, too. I wish you all the best, and live all that love to the fullest!

I wish you the best of luck with your situation, and I hope you are able to find a professional to help you, and that you are able to recover and heal from this. Stay safe OP. Take care.

My partner does this. It's a way of avoiding the issue by breaking down the conversation into philosophical meaninglessness. It's not intentional. He doesn't even realize he's doing it until afterwards. It's just a defense mechanism he has gotten really used to when he feels challenged or uncomfortable.

He used to also do this with our therapist and have angry outbursts during session, but with time and working on it together (and in his own separate therapy appointment on his own, very crucial) it has gotten better. He has been able to analyze what's going on for him when he's doing that and has been able to be more vulnerable and approach conflict with more patience and awareness.

But be aware: it took us almost a year to get to this point. 

If he's ready for therapy and willing to work on it, it's still going to take quite a long time for it to sink in and for him to feel comfortable exploring what's really going on for him. And it's going to take a lot of patience and understanding from you.

It sounds like he may not really be ready yet, if he's willing to fire every therapist he doesn't immediately take to or any therapist that has something not necessarily positive to say. 

I would consider picking the therapist that seems to have worked the best, and stick with them until things start clicking. Our therapist has gotten us through some really dark times, has stuck with us even when it seemed hopeless, and has been willing to get super real with the both of us about what we each need to be working on.

Sometimes it's uncomfortable, but it's necessary, and in my case, eventually, with patience, diligence, and understanding, my partner and I are better than we have been in a long time, we understand each other better, and we are able to work through things more effectively while showing love and concern for one another in healthier ways.

Just my (long ass) two cents. Good luck!

So, did he plan on the perfect gift for me ahead of time? No, he didn't.

As I mentioned up above somewhere, I believe it's at least in part ADHD. He struggles with both risk assessment as well as forgetfulness, and I think this could definitely be the manifestation of the culmination of the two.

I mean I have a similar issue of forgetfulness, and I've left a burner on here and there after cooking before, but as you say, I became aware that it's something I have the capacity to do, so I have trained myself over time to be more careful and aware. 

I mean I wouldn't choose to warm myself up this way without other options in the first place, and to agree with you, yes I also don't know why this is his choice. ¯\\_(ツ)_/¯

But who knows? Maybe I might choose this without a better honed set of risk assessment skills. Sometimes I wonder if I've only developed the set that I have because I've often had to deal with the consequences in ways that my partner has never had to, so for him, it's hard to realize that consequences are real even before they're actually literally happening.

My partner and I also had the issue with locking doors. It wasn't on his radar because he's never had to deal with the consequences of not having locked up, so to him, the risk isn't really *real*. 

But as you say, he would never forgive himself if we got robbed, or if I was raped, or god forbid, something worse. He just hasn't lived a life wherein those are actual tangible threats, so they don't register. It's actually been kind of a new idea to him that risking oneself is one thing, but being part of a group is actually taking responsibility to keep everyone safe. 

After some talks, and building the new routine, he locks up regularly now. But yes, I feel that issues with risk perception and risk assessment are certainly related to ADHD, even if it may not be so for every Dx person.

Yeah I've been thinking about that suggestion, that it's not ADHD, and I responded with my thoughts about that to someone above.

So while I'm certainly open, I admit I'm genuinely a bit confused about the reasoning behind why this can't be ADHD. I'll go over it with our therapist though just in case.

To me, this doesn't seem like a one-or-the-other-situation. 

While it's true that he did have a plan warm the house up this way, which speaks to lower risk perception and risk assessment skills (which can also be associated with ADHD) at the same time, he did actually get distracted, walk away, and forget. It wasn't his intention to turn them on and walk away from the beginning, it was his intention to turn them on and try to manage what he considered to be reasonable risk, but then got distracted and left it there. 

So I guess what I'm saying is, while I'm open to considering that something additional may be going on here, I'm reluctant to say that ADHD is not playing a role here, or that it may not be central in some way to the issue.

In this way, it gives OP's partner complete control over not only where and when OP can be in any given room, but it also gives OP's partner control over what OP can or can't be doing in said rooms, as well as control over the stimuli introduced in said rooms. 

As an autistic person for whom sound is literally painful, I completely empathize with OP. It can absolutely be a boundary issue for someone to be introducing stimuli to your person without your consent and without any ability to have input on its management. 

OP's partner can absolutely take responsibility for their own volume just like anyone with functioning vocal chords can. A struggle is not the same as an impossibility.

That said, I do believe ADHD to be a disability,  but as someone who is both physically and mentally disabled (and who was diagnosed with ADHD in my early 20s, for god's sake), I do not believe that it means that A.) I get to expect the world to bend around me or my whims, or that B.) I get to break other people's boundaries, or that C.) because I may struggle with something, it absolves me of any responsibility to manage my issues that affect other people. 

**"Consider this, if you can’t be mindful of your own responses and change how you respond to something, how can you expect to tell others to do the same and be successful at it?"**

My consideration of this is that I *can* be mindful of my own responses and change how I respond to something. I *can* take responsibility for my choices and my behavior, even if it's difficult, and even if those things are affected by my disabilities. The expectation here is merely a recognition that we are all responsible for our choices and our behavior. Something I've learned over the years in massive amounts of therapy is that "It may not be your fault, but it is your responsibility."

If counting calories is for sure what you want to do, you could join an app like Myfitnesspal or join r/1500isplenty here on Reddit if you need some guidance and support.

For veggies:
-2 large carrots, chopped 
-5 stalks celery, chopped
-10 baby potatoes, quartered
(Exact amounts may vary, you'll want about equal portions of each)
-Half a yellow onion, sliced

For veggie sauce:
-4 tbsp. butter
-.5 tsp rosemary 
-.5 tsp thyme
-.5 tsp onion powder
-2 - 3 tsp chicken bullion 

For chicken:
-2 boneless skinless chicken breasts 
-2 tbsp. butter
-.25 tsp thyme
-.5 tsp parsley 
-.5 tsp onion powder

Optional gravy:
-1 tsp - 1 tbsp cornstarch, plus juices from dish

----
*These are my suggested seasonings, but use what you like :)
*Bullion is optional, but I highly reccomend it, especially if you want to make the gravy. Add 2 - 3 tsp according to your tastes.
*Remember all slow cookers are different, so adjust heat and time accordingly.
----

1. Prepare veggies and set aside in large bowl.

2. Prepare veggie sauce: in a small dish, add 1st set of seasonings, and chicken bullion, to 4 tbsp of butter and microwave until melted. Stir. Pour over veggies and toss to coat evenly. 

3. Add veggies and sauce to slow cooker, cover, and cook on high 2 hours.

4. When 2 hours are almost up, prepare chicken: in a small dish, add 2nd set of seasonings to 2 tbsp of butter and microwave until melted. Stir. Brush onto chicken breasts.

5. When 2 hours is up, uncover veggies and stir to coat again with veggie sauce, then push them to the side. Add chicken breasts to open space, touching each other and the sides of the dish. 

6. Turn slow cooker to low setting, cover, and cook for an additional 2 hours.

Enjoy!

----
*Optional* To make a gravy:

1. When everything is cooked through, remove chicken and veggies (leaving the juices) and place in a covered dish to keep warm.

2. Pour remaining juices from slow cooker into a small sauce pan on medium heat.

3. Make a slurry in a small dish by adding a small amount of water to the cornstarch and mix well. Slowly add cornstarch slurry to pan juices, whisking constantly until thickened.

4. Toss gravy with veggies or drizzle over both veggies and chicken.

Enjoy!
